docs.title: Agential Control
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Agential control refers to the ability to adjust the execution of an action as the performance unfolds, a key component of being skilled that distinguishes skills from habits. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this capacity is fundamental to human agency and distinguishes skilled activity from habitual responses to environmental triggers.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text:
The concept builds on philosophical work distinguishing skills from habits:

  • Skills require control over initiating the task, whereas habits are merely elicited in response to environmental triggers
  • As agency develops, the balance between automaticity and control shifts through a process of tuning and attuning
  • To cultivate a skill is to develop flexible links between thought and action that continue to evolve even after expertise has been achieved

As Ferdman explains: "The implication is that an agent who performs out of habit, in response to triggers in the environment, is less skilled compared to the agent who has full control over initiating the activity."

docs.title: Plan-Forming vs. Plan-Following
docs.text:
Agential control is particularly evident in the distinction between plan-forming and plan-following:

  • Plan-forming: Requires exercising agential control over both the settling function (deciding between options) and coordination function (organizing different types of plans) of practical rationality
  • Plan-following: Involves merely responding to triggers in the environment without initiating the planning activity

This distinction is critical when evaluating AI personal assistants (APAs), which can shift users from plan-formers to plan-followers by providing pre-constructed plans that users merely execute.

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
In market research contexts, agential control manifests in:

  • Researchers initiating research questions rather than merely responding to AI-suggested topics
  • Analysts adjusting methodology in response to emerging data patterns rather than rigidly following pre-determined protocols
  • Moderators adapting interview techniques in real-time based on participant responses rather than strictly following scripted questions
  • Strategists developing novel research approaches to address unique business challenges rather than applying standardized templates

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine agential control in market research through:

  • Automated research design tools that generate complete study protocols without researcher initiation
  • AI assistants that provide pre-constructed analysis paths, reducing opportunities for researchers to develop their own analytical approaches
  • Recommendation systems that suggest research topics based on past behavior rather than encouraging novel question formulation
  • Reporting tools that automatically generate insights without requiring researchers to engage in the interpretation process

docs.title: Implications for Skill Development
docs.text:
The erosion of agential control has significant implications for market research skill development:

  • Without opportunities to initiate research activities, junior researchers cannot develop the practical wisdom necessary for complex decision-making
  • Reduced experience in plan-forming diminishes researchers' ability to handle unexpected research challenges
  • Over-reliance on pre-constructed research paths limits the development of creative capacities needed for innovative research design

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: AI Adoption Intensity Terciles is a methodology developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to categorize firms based on the intensity of their AI adoption, measured by the PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) metric.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. Firms are classified as AI adopters when they have three consecutive months of at least $100 in AI vendor spending
  2. Adoption intensity is measured as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over the first three months after adoption
  3. Among treated firms, PEPM values are sorted and divided into three equal groups (terciles):
  4. High intensity: top tercile (most intensive AI adopters)
  5. Medium intensity: middle tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom tercile (least intensive AI adopters)
  7. For analysis, firms are often grouped as:
  8. High intensity: top tercile
  9. Low intensity: bottom two terciles combined

docs.title: Rationale for Tercile Approach
docs.text:
• Allows researchers to examine differential impacts of AI adoption based on intensity
  • Reveals that not all AI adopters experience the same employment effects
  • Helps address selection bias by comparing firms with similar eventual adoption intensity
  • Shows that substantial employment gains are concentrated among high-intensity adopters

docs.title: Key Findings Using Intensity Terciles
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters grew total employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • High-intensity gains emerged gradually over 18-24 months, suggesting a learning curve
  • Employment gains were broad across roles for high-intensity adopters (engineering, sales, administration, customer service)

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: This methodology revealed a critical insight often missed in prior research: AI's labor market effects differ substantially based on adoption intensity. Studies that treat all adopters the same may miss these nuanced patterns.

docs.title: Ramp-Revelio Methodology
docs.text:
The study introduces the AI Spend Per Employee Methodology (PEPM):

  1. Adoption definition: Three consecutive months of ≥$100 AI vendor spend
  2. Intensity measure: PEPM = (sum of first 3 months' AI spend) / (3 × baseline headcount)
  3. Intensity stratification: Low (bottom two PEPM terciles), High (top PEPM tercile)
  4. Comparison design: Later adopters within same intensity group

This approach overcomes four critical limitations of prior methods:

  1. Direct observation: Measures actual adoption behavior rather than theoretical exposure
  2. Timing precision: Captures exact adoption month rather than imputed timing
  3. Intensity dimension: Reveals differential effects by adoption intensity
  4. Firm-level specificity: Avoids occupational aggregation that masks firm differences

docs.title: Observed Spending Threshold
docs.text: The $100/month threshold excludes one-off experiments while capturing sustained adoption, addressing the "Is this really AI adoption?" question that plagues survey-based approaches.

docs.title: PEPM Metric
docs.text: Using baseline headcount in the denominator makes intensity comparable across firm sizes and keeps employee scale predetermined relative to adoption timing.

docs.title: Staggered Treatment Design
docs.text: The Callaway-Sant'Anna framework accounts for heterogeneous treatment timing, avoiding biases in traditional event-study approaches.

docs.title: Evidence of Impact
docs.text: This methodological innovation revealed findings invisible to exposure-based studies: - Only high-intensity adopters (+10.2% headcount growth) showed significant employment effects - Entry-level roles grew 12.0% among high-intensity adopters, contradicting exposure-based predictions - Effects concentrated in Information sector (+13.4% growth), not uniformly distributed

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological shift has critical implications:

  • Vendor evaluation: Must measure actual usage intensity, not just adoption status
  • Impact assessment: Requires tracking spending patterns over time, not binary adoption
  • Benchmarking: Industry comparisons must account for intensity differences
  • ROI calculation: Benefits appear only above critical intensity thresholds

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This innovation directly addresses the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and explains the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies observed across research. It represents a critical advance over the pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index used in pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer.

docs.title: Practical Implementation
docs.text:
For market research organizations, adopting this methodological innovation means: - Tracking actual AI spending rather than adoption claims - Measuring intensity through normalized spending metrics - Comparing against firms with similar pre-adoption characteristics - Focusing on sustained usage patterns rather than initial adoption

Without these methodological improvements, organizations risk misattributing effects or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns—precisely what the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study demonstrates.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The substantial pre-existing differences between AI adopters and non-adopters that complicate causal inference in AI impact studies. As rigorously documented in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, these selection effects mean AI adopters were already distinct from non-adopters before AI adoption, creating significant methodological challenges.

docs.title: Key Evidence
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study demonstrates dramatic pre-adoption differences:

Characteristic AI Adopters Never Adopters Difference Headcount (mean) 144.2 103.9 +40.3* Engineering share 26.8% 18.6% +8.2* Entry-level share 42.1% 50.4% -8.3* YoY growth (median) 6.0% 1.6% +4.4* Mean salary $110,346 $93,847 +$16,499* Tech-adjacent sector 54.2% 25.9% +28.3* VC-backed 34.0% 9.5% +24.5*

*Statistically significant at p<0.01

docs.title: Methodological Implications
docs.text:
This selection bias creates three critical challenges for AI impact research:

  1. Confounded comparisons: Simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons conflate AI effects with pre-existing differences
  2. Pre-trend divergence: Adopters were already on different growth trajectories before adoption (see Figure 4 in Ramp-Revelio study)
  3. Sector concentration: AI adoption heavily concentrated in Information (53.7%), Finance (43.6%), and Professional Services (36.0%)

docs.title: Addressing the Bias
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study employs sophisticated methods to address selection bias:

  • Preferred comparison: Later adopters within the same eventual intensity group
  • Sector fixed effects: Controlling for industry composition differences
  • Event-time analysis: Tracking pre-treatment parallel trends
  • Intensity stratification: Separating low vs. high adoption intensity effects

This approach revealed that only high-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no significant change.

docs.title: Contrast with Exposure-Based Studies
docs.text: This selection bias explains why exposure-based studies (like pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer) often produce different findings than spending-based studies: - Exposure scores cannot distinguish firms that adopt AI from those that don't - They assume uniform adoption effects across firms with identical workforce composition - They miss the critical intensity dimension revealed by actual spending data

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This concept has profound implications for insights organizations:

  • Vendor selection: AI tools adopted by leading firms may reflect pre-existing advantages rather than causal benefits
  • Implementation strategy: Success depends on organizational readiness, not just tool adoption
  • Impact measurement: Must account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI initiatives
  • Benchmarking: Comparing against industry averages without controlling for selection effects is misleading

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This concept is central to understanding the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies problem and represents a key ai-adoption-methodological-innovation addressed by the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study. It explains why the employment gains documented in that study are concentrated among high-intensity adopters in specific sectors, rather than across all AI adopters.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, addressing selection bias requires: - Never comparing AI adopters to non-adopters without controlling for pre-existing differences - Measuring adoption intensity (PEPM) rather than binary adoption status - Using staggered adoption timing in evaluation designs - Focusing on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact

Without these precautions, organizations risk attributing pre-existing advantages to AI adoption or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns.

docs.title: Ai democratization
docs.text: AI democratization refers to the process where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI democratization describes how artificial intelligence makes advanced capabilities accessible by automating complex expert tasks, thereby reducing expertise requirements for certain occupations. As quantified in Figure 2 of the PwC 2026 report, this process affects 52% of global job postings. Concrete examples include [[recruiters]] (AI automates CV screening while humans handle contract negotiation) and [[inventory-clerks]] (AI manages stock optimization while humans perform physical movement). Figure 3 demonstrates democratization is particularly strong in high AI exposure jobs, where expertise requirements decrease significantly. Crucially, Figure 11 reveals that despite reduced expertise demands, democratized roles maintain high epoch-score (0.48), indicating continued reliance on human capabilities for remaining tasks—often involving physical dexterity, adaptability, or interpersonal skills. The report warns that while democratization expands job accessibility (e.g., enabling non-experts to perform data analysis), it may compress career ladders and reduce skill development opportunities without targeted interventions. This concept represents one of two primary pathways (alongside ai-professionalization) in AI's labor market restructuring. Organizations can leverage democratization through the ai-job-future-framework's 'Supply and Demand' dimension, redesigning roles to balance AI efficiency with human execution. The trend is accelerating post-2022, as shown in Figure 9's widening skill transformation gap, requiring proactive workforce planning to ensure equitable access to emerging opportunities in democratized roles.

docs.title: AI Deskilling as a Structural Problem
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: AI deskilling as a structural problem refers to the phenomenon where AI systems undermine human capacities through systemic conditions that create environments hostile to capacity cultivation, rather than through individual failings. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this perspective moves beyond framing deskilling as a matter of individual responsibility to recognize how AI's influence creates systemic conditions that inhibit the development and exercise of human capacities.

docs.title: Core Argument
docs.text:
The structural perspective on AI deskilling makes these key arguments:

  1. Beyond individual responsibility: Framing deskilling as a matter of individual responsibility—expecting people to simply will themselves to cultivate 'the arts of personhood'—overlooks crucial structural aspects of the problem

  2. Environmental dependence: We develop and exercise our epistemic, moral, social, and creative capacities in response to our social and material environment; a deficient environment can lead to deskilling of our core human capacities

  3. Capacity impoverishment: Inadequate development of core human capacities leads to "capacity impoverishment," which diminishes us as humans and undermines our flourishing

  4. Structural evaluation: AI applications should be evaluated based on their conduciveness or hostility to capacity cultivation

As Ferdman states: "Rather than focusing only on how human agents ought to engage with AI tools, we should also ask what kind of socio-technical environments would be best for the cultivation of our personhood."

docs.title: Capacity-Skill Framework
docs.text:
The paper introduces a capacity-skill framework to understand human capacities:

  • Being capacity-skilled means having agential control over the human capacities, obtained through a process of intersubjective, embodied habituation
  • This manifests in competent exercise of the human capacities, as well as societal shared valuing of the capacities
  • Capacity deskilling manifests as impoverishment of the capacities: limited agential control, diminished habituation process, and devaluation of the capacities

docs.title: Structural Mechanisms
docs.text:
The paper identifies several structural mechanisms through which AI creates capacity-hostile environments:

  • Narrow field of affordances: AI systems restrict, limit, or create a narrow field of affordances for capacity development and exercise
  • Automation bias: Offloading tasks to AI reduces opportunities for habituation and skill development
  • Disembodiment: AI-mediated interactions reduce opportunities for embodied skill development
  • Reduced intersubjectivity: AI systems diminish opportunities for shared valuing of capacities through mentor-mentee relationships

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
The structural perspective on AI deskilling has significant implications for the market research industry:

  • The human-operating-model-gap between rapidly advancing AI capabilities and slower adaptation of human systems is not merely an individual skills gap but a structural environmental problem
  • The entry-level-squeeze phenomenon reflects how AI automation creates capacity-hostile environments for developing foundational research skills
  • Organizations must design capacity-conducive environments that preserve opportunities for developing human-intensive skills
  • The industry's value proposition increasingly depends on cultivating human capacities that AI cannot replicate

docs.title: Ai job future framework
docs.text: A framework of four questions to analyze how AI is reshaping specific occupations, developed by PwC in their 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The AI Job Future Framework, introduced in Figure 6 of PwC's 2026 report, provides a structured methodology to assess AI's occupational impact through four critical questions: (1) Expertise: How is AI changing required human expertise? (e.g., democratization reduces expertise needs while professionalization increases them); (2) Supply and Demand: How might job demand and worker supply shift as AI reshapes roles?; (3) AI's limitations: Where is human oversight needed for quality control or atypical cases?; and (4) Environmental forces: How do regulations, business bottlenecks, or ethics constrain AI adoption? The report demonstrates the framework's application across diverse occupations: For [[pharmacists]], AI handles prescription processing (Expertise shift) but humans manage patient counseling (AI's limitations); for [[software-developers]], AI generates code but humans focus on architecture (Environmental forces). Figure 9 validates the framework by showing how high AI exposure roles undergo 2.2x faster skill changes, directly addressing the Supply and Demand dimension. Organizations using this tool can anticipate skill shifts, redesign roles, and develop targeted training—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' (Figure 12). The framework also explains wage dynamics: roles requiring human oversight of AI (Question 3) command higher premiums, as seen in Figure 15's 62% average AI skill premium. By systematically addressing these questions, employers can transform AI disruption into opportunity, while workers identify future-proof career paths in the evolving labor market. This methodology has become essential for strategic workforce planning in the AI era.

AI professionalization refers to the process where AI automates less expert tasks, leaving more expert tasks for humans. This phenomenon represents one pathway through which AI reshapes occupations, increasing the premium on specialized human expertise.

The mrii-2026-market-research-study provides compelling evidence of AI professionalization in the insights industry: - As AI handles routine analytical tasks, value is shifting upstream toward strategic functions - Insights teams must evolve from delivering answers to shaping decisions, driving growth, and influencing strategy - Pam Forbus of [[mondelez]] states: "AI will increasingly answer questions, deliver insights, execute projects, and support stakeholders faster and at lower cost than ever before. That doesn't diminish the role of insights teams; it fundamentally changes it."

The value-chain-shift concept further explains this dynamic - as AI makes answers faster and cheaper, the answers themselves become less differentiated, pushing value creation toward higher-order strategic functions.

A critical finding from the MRII study reveals a professionalization paradox: - Professionals prioritize learning technical AI skills - Leaders value business acumen, communication, and strategic influence more highly

This disconnect threatens to undermine the professionalization process, as organizations may automate tasks without adequately developing the human capabilities needed for the elevated roles.

docs.title: Capacity-Conducive Environments
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Capacity-conducive environments are settings that actively encourage the development and exercise of human capacities through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these environments provide sufficient invitations for valuable activities that trigger the competent exercise of human capacities, in contrast to capacity-hostile environments that restrict such opportunities.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
Capacity-conducive environments typically exhibit these features:

  • Rich affordance landscape: Provide diverse action possibilities that encourage development of multiple capacities simultaneously
  • Embodied interaction opportunities: Facilitate physical presence and sensory experience in skill development
  • Intersubjective learning: Support mentor-mentee relationships where both parties share intentions and develop "shared valuing" of capacities
  • Agential control cultivation: Encourage users to initiate activities rather than merely respond to environmental triggers
  • Responsibility ownership: Create contexts where users must take accountability for outcomes, enabling self-critique and growth

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
In market research contexts, capacity-conducive environments include:

  • Research settings that preserve opportunities for human-to-human interaction in qualitative studies, maintaining the embodied component of understanding participant perspectives
  • Team structures that encourage collaborative sense-making through shared physical spaces or high-fidelity virtual environments
  • Training programs that incorporate gradual habituation through successive trials, learning from mistakes, and refinement of action
  • Processes that maintain researcher involvement in the full research cycle, from question formulation to interpretation, rather than offloading segments to AI
  • Community spaces (physical or virtual) that encourage researchers to share experiences and develop shared understanding of research values

docs.title: Structural Design Principles
docs.text:
As Ferdman explains, capacity-conducive environments should incorporate these design principles:

  1. Embodied engagement: Include public goods like community centers, quality public spaces, and libraries that encourage structured and unstructured embodied interactions
  2. Intersubjective valuing: Create contexts where researchers can develop shared understanding of the value of core capacities
  3. Gradual habituation: Structure skill development through progressive challenges that build on previous experiences
  4. Volitional encouragement: Design systems that require and reward effort, perseverance, and growth rather than expecting "virtuous superheroes"

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text: The transition to AI-augmented market research requires deliberate design of capacity-conducive environments to preserve the human capacities that differentiate quality insights. Organizations must balance AI adoption with maintaining opportunities for researchers to develop the epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities that constitute human flourishing. This is particularly critical as entry-level positions face increasing pressure from AI automation (entry-level-squeeze), making structured capacity development more essential than ever.

docs.title: Capacity-Hostile Environments
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Capacity-hostile environments are settings that restrict, limit, or create a narrow field of affordances for the development and exercise of core human capacities. These environments afford opportunities for shallow skilling in human capacities while restricting opportunities for fuller, well-rounded development and exercise of capacities. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, such environments systematically undermine the process of capacity cultivation through structural conditions rather than individual failings.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
Capacity-hostile environments typically exhibit these features:

  • Narrow field of affordances: Provide limited action possibilities that restrict opportunities for developing human capacities
  • Reduced embodied interaction: Favor disembodied digital engagement over physical presence and sensory experience
  • Diminished intersubjectivity: Limit opportunities for shared valuing of capacities through mentor-mentee relationships
  • Automation bias: Encourage offloading of decision-making to AI systems, reducing opportunities for exercising agential control
  • Responsibility displacement: Enable users to shift accountability for failed plans to AI systems, reducing opportunities for self-critique and growth

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
In market research contexts, capacity-hostile environments emerge when:

  • AI tools automate routine data analysis tasks, depriving researchers of "routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature" (Lee et al. 2025)
  • Chatbots replace human interaction in customer interviews, undermining the development of empathy and social capacities
  • Automated reporting systems eliminate opportunities for researchers to exercise creative capacities in presenting findings
  • AI personal assistants (APAs) replace the process of self-deliberation in research planning, shifting users from plan-formers to plan-followers

docs.title: Structural Mechanisms
docs.text:
As Ferdman explains, capacity-hostile environments operate through several structural mechanisms:

  1. Affordance shrinkage: Systematic reduction in action possibilities that discourages users from finding compensatory pathways
  2. Habituation disruption: Interference with the gradual process of skill development through practice and feedback
  3. Shared valuing erosion: Diminished opportunities for learning the value of capacities through relationships with others
  4. Embodiment limitation: Reduced physical presence in interactions critical for social and moral capacity development

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text: The proliferation of capacity-hostile environments in market research threatens the industry's core value proposition. As human-intensive skills like empathy, creativity, and face-to-face presence become increasingly important in AI-exposed roles (human-intensive-skills), environments that undermine these capacities directly threaten research quality. Organizations must actively design capacity-conducive environments that preserve opportunities for researchers to develop the human capacities that differentiate human insight from AI-generated analysis.

docs.title: Creative Capacities
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-18 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Creative capacities are the human capacities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities enable innovation and adaptation and constitute a core component of human flourishing in market research contexts.

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text:
Creative capacities exhibit these critical features:

  • Novel combination: Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas
  • Conceptual transformation: Transforming a conceptual space without relying merely on luck, accidents, or mechanical procedures
  • Innovation: Generating new approaches, methods, and insights
  • Adaptation: Adjusting to novel situations and unexpected events

As Ferdman explains: "The capacity for creativity involves making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas, transforming a conceptual space (Boden 2004), without relying merely on luck, accidents, or mechanical procedures (Gaut, 2010)."

docs.title: Role in Life-Planning and Research
docs.text:
Creative capacities play a critical role in both life-planning and market research:

  • Planning requires the ability to reconsider and respond to novel situations, surprises, and unexpected events
  • Research design often demands creative approaches to address unique business challenges
  • Data interpretation benefits from creative connections between seemingly unrelated findings
  • Solution development requires innovative applications of research insights
  • Navigating research constraints demands creative problem-solving

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine creative capacities through:

  • Providing standardized research templates that reduce opportunities for novel approach development
  • Generating conventional insights that limit researchers' exposure to unexpected connections
  • Reducing opportunities to respond to research surprises through automated analysis paths
  • Diminishing the need for creative problem-solving through AI-assisted solutions
  • Creating environments that favor established patterns over novel combinations

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
In market research contexts, creative capacities manifest through:

  • Developing innovative research methodologies for complex business questions
  • Making unexpected connections between data points that reveal new insights
  • Adapting research approaches in response to participant feedback or unexpected findings
  • Creating novel visualizations that communicate complex findings effectively
  • Designing research instruments that capture nuanced human behaviors

docs.title: Implications for the Industry
docs.text:
The erosion of creative capacities has significant implications for market research:

  • Reduced ability to develop innovative research approaches for novel business challenges
  • Diminished capacity to make unexpected connections that reveal breakthrough insights
  • Weakened ability to adapt research methods in response to changing market conditions
  • Increased homogeneity in research findings as creative exploration diminishes
  • Contribution to the human-operating-model-gap between AI capabilities and human creativity

docs.title: Developmental Perfectionism
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-15 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Developmental Perfectionism is a neo-Aristotelian approach to human flourishing where flourishing is understood as a complex, unified, and well-rounded life. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this philosophical framework provides the foundation for understanding why capacity-deskilling is harmful to human beings.

docs.title: Core Principles
docs.text:
Developmental Perfectionism is characterized by these key principles:

  • Complex unity: Human flourishing is not merely the sum of individual goods but a complex, unified whole
  • Well-rounded life: Flourishing involves the balanced development and exercise of multiple human capacities
  • Intrinsic value: Activities yield outcomes that have intrinsic value like knowledge, beauty, morality, and friendship
  • Capacity manifestation: The competent exercise of human capacities is the manifestation of intrinsically valuable goods
  • Constitutive relationship: Human capacities are constitutive of flourishing, not merely instrumental to it

As Ferdman explains: "Developmental Perfectionism neatly captures why deskilling is bad: capacity-deskilling is bad because our human capacities are constitutive of our flourishing. Impoverished capacities (i.e., capacity-deskilling), therefore, lead to impoverished lives."

docs.title: Why Deskilling is Harmful
docs.text:
The framework explains why capacity-deskilling is harmful:

  • The value of an achievement is gained from the competent exercise of capacities involved, not merely from the outcome
  • For example, the value of reaching the summit of Mt. Everest comes from the competent exercise of climbing capacities, not merely from being there (e.g., via helicopter)
  • Impoverished capacities lead to impoverished lives because human capacities are constitutive of flourishing
  • Capacity-deskilling diminishes us as human beings by undermining our abilities in the 'arts of personhood'

docs.title: Distinction from Skill Obsolescence
docs.text:
Developmental Perfectionism distinguishes between:

  • Benign skill obsolescence: Where technological developments free up time and resources for cultivating other skills (e.g., hunting, basket-weaving, or coding)
  • Harmful capacity-deskilling: The deskilling of core human capacities—to know, create, form meaningful relationships, and use our willpower—which diminishes us as humans

As Ferdman states: "Whereas deskilling of activities like hunting, basket-weaving or coding may be innocuous, capacity-deskilling should always be a cause for worry."

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
The Developmental Perfectionism framework has significant implications for the market research industry:

  • The industry's value increasingly depends on human capacities that constitute flourishing rather than easily automated skills
  • Organizations must preserve opportunities for developing the complex, unified set of capacities required for quality insights
  • The human-intensive-skills that differentiate human researchers from AI are constitutive of professional flourishing
  • AI adoption strategies should be evaluated based on whether they support or undermine the development of researchers' constitutive capacities

docs.title: Embodiment in Skilling
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Embodiment in skilling refers to the essential role of physical presence and sensory experience in the development of human capacities, particularly social and moral skills. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this dimension is critical for cultivating capacities that require embodied interaction and cannot be fully developed in disembodied environments.

docs.title: Philosophical Foundation
docs.text:
The concept builds on the Enactive Approach in cognition, which posits that:

  • Embodied 'participatory sense-making' is constitutive of social cognition
  • Social interaction itself and its emergent dynamics constitute an essential part of the cognitive process
  • Meaning is generated and transformed in the interplay between unfolding interaction and individuals engaged
  • Agents come to apprehend other perceived bodies as being similar loci of embodied subjectivity

As Ferdman explains: "Without being embodied in a social interaction—without the return of the gaze of the other—we would be hard-pressed to recognize them spontaneously as moral agents. The spontaneity of recognizing the other as moral agent is inherent in the embodied interaction."

docs.title: Critical Role in Capacity Development
docs.text:
Embodiment plays these essential roles in developing human capacities:

  • Moral attention: Requires perceiving others as embodied beings similar to ourselves through voice and gaze
  • Social cognition: Depends on embodied understanding where agents recognize others as similar loci of subjectivity
  • Shared valuing: Creates shared history and participatory sense-making regarding both skill products and the skill itself
  • Friendship development: Enables meaningful relationships that are diminished in technologically mediated virtue friendships

docs.title: Threats from Disembodied Environments
docs.text:
Disembodied environments pose significant challenges to capacity development:

  • Without embodied interaction, recognizing others as moral agents requires more mental effort
  • Technologically mediated virtue friendships require more discipline for a diminished experience
  • Disembodied interactions make it harder to form meaningful friendships
  • The absence of embodied cues limits opportunities for developing social and moral capacities

As Ferdman notes: "disembodied interactions make it harder to form meaningful friendship because technologically mediated virtue friendships require more discipline for a diminished experience."

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
In market research contexts, embodiment in skilling is critical for:

  • Qualitative research where moderators develop rapport with participants through embodied presence
  • Team collaboration where shared physical space enables spontaneous idea generation and refinement
  • Client presentations where embodied communication conveys nuance and builds trust
  • Ethnographic research where physical presence in context is essential for understanding cultural phenomena
  • Training programs that incorporate role-playing and embodied practice of research techniques

docs.title: Implications for AI Adoption
docs.text:
The shift toward AI-mediated research practices has significant implications for embodiment in skilling:

  • Remote research methods reduce opportunities for embodied interaction with participants
  • AI analysis tools diminish the need for researchers to develop embodied understanding of data patterns
  • Automated reporting systems reduce opportunities for researchers to practice embodied presentation skills
  • Virtual collaboration tools, while valuable, cannot fully replicate the richness of embodied team interaction

docs.title: Entry level squeeze
docs.text: The entry-level squeeze describes the growing pressure on traditional entry-level positions in knowledge work as AI capabilities automate foundational tasks that historically served as training grounds for developing professional expertise.

docs.title: Capacity Development Challenges for Entry-Level Workers
docs.text: While recent evidence shows entry-level headcount is growing among high-intensity AI adopters, the nature of entry-level work is changing in ways that may affect capacity development for junior professionals.

docs.title: Deskilling Risks in Entry-Level Roles
docs.text:
The ai-deskilling-structural-problem framework reveals several risks for entry-level workers:

  • Reduced habituation opportunities: When AI automates routine tasks, entry-level workers lose "the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature" (Lee et al. 2025)
  • Shallow skill development: Entry into professions may become more superficial without proper mentoring
  • Disembodied learning: Digital workflows may limit embodied interaction necessary for social capacity development
  • Affordance shrinkage: Systematic reduction in action possibilities for developing practical wisdom

docs.title: Structural Dimensions
docs.text:
These challenges are not merely individual responsibility issues but stem from structural conditions:

"We develop and exercise our epistemic, moral, social, and creative capacities in response to our social and material environment" (Ferdman 2026). When entry-level environments become [[capacity-hostile]], junior professionals may struggle to develop the "arts of personhood" required for long-term success.

docs.title: Evidence from Research
docs.text: Studies show that young people growing up with digital tools already struggle with "everyday but essential" skills like empathy, time management, speaking to others, problem-solving and critical thinking (Halliday 2025). AI tools like artificial-personal-assistants could potentially exacerbate this deskilling.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these findings suggest:

  • Entry-level training programs must intentionally preserve opportunities for capacity development
  • Mentorship relationships are crucial for counteracting AI-mediated deskilling
  • Workflows should balance AI augmentation with human skill development
  • Organizations should design capacity-conducive environments for junior staff

The structural perspective emphasizes that "we cannot expect agents to be what Mitcham (2024) calls 'virtuous superheroes' and properly cultivate their human capacities if their social environment does not value the full maturation of these capacities."

See capacity-conducive-environments and habituation-process for related frameworks addressing these challenges.

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-18 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Epistemic capacities are the human capacities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding, including theoretical rationality and practical rationality (phronesis). As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are essential for navigating truth and making informed decisions, and constitute a core component of human flourishing.

docs.title: Theoretical Rationality
docs.text:
• Thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, and contemplating
  • Essential for knowledge acquisition and critical evaluation of information
  • Enables researchers to assess the validity and reliability of data sources
  • Critical for distinguishing between correlation and causation in research findings

docs.title: Practical Rationality (Phronesis)
docs.text:
• Doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason
  • Manifests in practical wisdom: knowing effective means to ends and possessing accurate understanding of situations
  • Includes discernment: correct understanding of how the good and the bad apply in particular circumstances
  • Necessary for critically reflecting on conceptions of a flourishing life and setting appropriate goals

As Ferdman explains: "To be well motivated is not enough, to have practical wisdom is to be an effective and savvy agent in the real world, equipped with valuable life experience."

docs.title: Role in Life-Planning
docs.text:
Epistemic capacities play a critical role in life-planning:

  • Exercise of theoretical rationality in self-deliberation on values and goals
  • Application of practical wisdom regarding coordinating goals and intentions with actions
  • Critical reflection on conceptions of a flourishing life to set appropriate research goals
  • Assessment of testimony from others in research contexts

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine epistemic capacities through:

  • Providing instant answers that bypass the gradual development of research judgment
  • Reducing opportunities for researchers to exercise theoretical rationality in forming beliefs
  • Diminishing the need to develop practical wisdom through automated decision support
  • Creating environments where researchers outsource critical thinking to AI systems
  • Contributing to the erosion of critical thinking, decision-making, and analytical reasoning documented in multiple studies

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
In market research contexts, epistemic capacities manifest through:

  • Theoretical rationality in evaluating research methodologies and data quality
  • Practical wisdom in determining appropriate research approaches for specific business challenges
  • Critical assessment of AI-generated insights for validity and relevance
  • Discernment in applying research findings to complex business situations
  • Self-deliberation on research ethics and professional standards

docs.title: Implications for the Industry
docs.text:
The erosion of epistemic capacities has significant implications for market research:

  • Reduced ability to critically evaluate AI-generated insights
  • Diminished capacity to develop novel research approaches for complex problems
  • Weakened ability to translate research findings into actionable business recommendations
  • Contribution to the human-operating-model-gap between AI capabilities and human judgment
  • Increased vulnerability to research biases when critical thinking is outsourced to AI

docs.title: Habituation Process
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The habituation process refers to the gradual development of skill through practice, involving inculcation through continued attunement to the demands of individual cases. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this process is essential for developing human capacities and cannot be shortcut through testimony or abstract principles alone.

docs.title: Key Characteristics
docs.text:
The habituation process exhibits these critical features:

  • Gradual progression: Moves through stages from novice to expert, with increasing sophistication and sensitivity to varying contexts
  • Experience-based: Requires considerable time and living, with refinement through successive trials and learning from mistakes
  • Non-repetitive: Involves growth rather than simple repetition, with each iteration building on previous experiences
  • Context-sensitive: Develops through attunement to the demands of individual cases rather than application of universal rules
  • Failure-embracing: Incorporates disappointment and failure as essential components of skill development

As Ferdman explains: "Habituation involves inculcation through continued attunement to the demands of individual cases; refinement of the action through successive trials and learning from mistakes. This includes encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure."

docs.title: Two Essential Components
docs.text: The habituation process comprises two interdependent dimensions:

docs.title: Intersubjectivity
docs.text:
• Requires mentorship where a guide instills not only mechanical aspects of the skill but also the value of the skill
  • Involves developing "shared valuing" of the skill through relationships with others
  • Occurs at societal scale through social practices that generate moral reasons for action
  • Depends on shared intentions between mentor and mentee that evolve into shared valuing of the skill

docs.title: Embodiment
docs.text:
• Necessitates physical presence and sensory experience in skill development
  • Relies on "embodied understanding" where agents recognize others as similar loci of embodied subjectivity
  • Enables "participatory sense-making" through the interplay between unfolding interaction and individuals engaged
  • Creates shared history and context that cannot be replicated in disembodied environments

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine the habituation process in market research through:

  • Automating routine research tasks that provide essential practice opportunities for developing cognitive skills
  • Providing instant answers that bypass the gradual process of developing research judgment
  • Reducing opportunities for learning from mistakes by preventing researchers from encountering and overcoming failures
  • Diminishing mentor-mentee relationships through automated guidance systems
  • Creating disembodied research environments that limit opportunities for embodied interaction

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
The erosion of proper habituation processes has significant consequences for the market research industry:

  • Junior researchers experience the entry-level-squeeze as AI automates foundational tasks that historically served as training grounds
  • Reduced opportunities for gradual skill development contribute to the seniorised-roles phenomenon where entry-level positions increasingly demand traditionally senior skills
  • Diminished mentor-mentee relationships undermine the transmission of tacit knowledge essential for research excellence
  • Disembodied research environments limit the development of social and moral capacities critical for ethical research practices

docs.title: Human Capacities
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-15 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Human capacities are core abilities that constitute human flourishing, including epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are fundamental to being human and can be undermined by AI systems through capacity-hostile environments.

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text:
• Theoretical rationality: Thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, contemplating
  • Practical rationality (phronesis): Doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason, manifesting in practical wisdom
  • Essential for knowledge acquisition, critical thinking, and sound judgment

docs.title: Social Capacities
docs.text:
• Moral capacity: Ability to make ethical judgments and act accordingly
  • Relational capacity: Ability to form meaningful relationships of friendship and love
  • Essential for social interaction, ethical research practices, and understanding human behavior

docs.title: Creative Capacities
docs.text:
• Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas
  • Transforming conceptual spaces without relying merely on luck, accidents, or mechanical procedures
  • Essential for innovative research design and novel insight generation

docs.title: Volitional Capacity
docs.text:
• The ability to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere and grow
  • Required to achieve intrinsically valuable goals
  • Treated as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities
  • Particularly important because developing other capacities is difficult and requires willpower

docs.title: Constitutive Nature
docs.text:
Human capacities are constitutive of flourishing rather than merely instrumental:

  • The competent exercise of capacities manifests intrinsically valuable goods
  • The value of achievements comes from the competent exercise of capacities involved
  • For example, the value of reaching Mt. Everest's summit comes from the competent exercise of climbing capacities, not merely from being there
  • Impoverished capacities lead to impoverished lives

As Ferdman explains: "The competent exercise of the human capacities is the manifestation of the achievement of the intrinsically valuable goods, making the capacities intrinsically valuable too."

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine human capacities through:

  • Creating capacity-hostile environments that restrict opportunities for capacity development
  • Automating routine tasks that provide essential practice for developing capacities
  • Reducing opportunities for embodied interaction critical for social and moral capacities
  • Diminishing intersubjective learning opportunities essential for shared valuing of capacities
  • Encouraging plan-following rather than plan-forming, reducing opportunities to exercise practical rationality

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
The concept of human capacities has significant implications for the market research industry:

  • The industry's value proposition increasingly depends on human capacities that AI cannot replicate
  • The human-intensive-skills that differentiate quality research are manifestations of these core capacities
  • Organizations must design capacity-conducive environments that preserve opportunities for developing these capacities
  • The entry-level-squeeze phenomenon threatens the development of these capacities among new researchers
  • The value-chain-shift in market research reflects a repositioning toward activities that leverage these core human capacities

docs.title: Human operating model gap
docs.text: The human operating model gap refers to the growing disparity between the rapid advancement of AI capabilities and the slower adaptation of human systems, processes, and skills required to leverage AI effectively within organizations.

docs.title: Workforce Composition Changes with AI Adoption
docs.text: Recent evidence reveals how AI adoption is reshaping workforce composition across roles, highlighting the growing gap between rapidly advancing AI capabilities and slower human system adaptation.

docs.title: Role-Specific Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study provides detailed evidence of how AI adoption affects different job functions:

  • Broad-based growth: High-intensity adopters showed growth across multiple roles:
  • Sales headcount: +10.3%
  • Administrative headcount: +7.8%
  • Engineering headcount: +7.3%
  • Customer service headcount: +6.3%

  • Scientist headcount: +5.6%

  • Entry-level expansion: Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% among high-intensity adopters

  • Managerial shifts: Manager-plus share fell by 1.52 percentage points despite overall growth

docs.title: Structural Workforce Shifts
docs.text:
These findings reveal several important patterns:

  1. Non-binary impact: AI adoption doesn't simply eliminate jobs but reshapes workforce composition
  2. Intensity matters: Only high-intensity adopters (top tercile of AI spend) showed significant growth
  3. Gradual emergence: Gains followed a learning curve, emerging 6-12 months after adoption
  4. Sector concentration: Effects were strongest in the Information sector

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these workforce shifts suggest:

  • AI is currently augmenting rather than replacing human capabilities in information work
  • Strategic AI investment may support growth across multiple functions
  • Entry-level positions may expand as firms scale with AI assistance
  • Workforce planning must account for the gradual nature of AI integration

The study notes that "the earliest signs of growth emerge roughly 6-12 months after adoption, perhaps after firms establish best practices, integrate AI tools into workflows, and are subsequently able to make new investments and hire staff."

docs.title: Bridging the Gap
docs.text:
To address the human operating model gap, market research firms should:

  • Develop AI adoption strategies that align with workforce development
  • Create pathways for employees to develop AI-augmented capabilities
  • Recognize that successful integration requires time for habituation
  • Design capacity-conducive environments that preserve opportunities for skill development

See value-chain-shift and ai-professionalization for related frameworks analyzing AI's impact on organizational structures.

docs.title: Intersubjectivity in Skilling
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-03 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Intersubjectivity in skilling refers to the shared understanding dimension of skill development, where learning occurs through relationships with others who guide and share the value of the skill. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this dimension is essential for cultivating human capacities, as it enables the transmission of both technical knowledge and the intrinsic value of the skill.

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text: Intersubjectivity in skilling comprises these critical elements:

docs.title: Mentor-Mentee Relationship
docs.text:
• A good mentor is typically necessary to cultivate the proper motivational structure for becoming skilled
  • Mentors instill not only mechanical aspects of the skill but, as importantly, the value of the skill
  • Through this relationship, the novice eventually comes to view the value of the skill as their own
  • Both mentor and mentee develop shared intentions that evolve into "shared valuing" of the skill

docs.title: Societal Dimension
docs.text:
• Social practices performed by groups or whole societies provide mentoring environments
  • Social practices generate moral reasons for action through constitutive aims or telos
  • Learning occurs through "the practices of the common life" as agents become responsive to what skillful action requires
  • Communities of practice create shared understanding regarding both the outputs of skilled activity and the skill itself

As Ferdman explains: "The process of habituation is intersubjective also on a societal scale. Social practices performed by groups or whole societies can provide a mentoring environment: the family, colleagues, citizens and so on."

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
In market research contexts, intersubjectivity in skilling manifests through:

  • Senior researchers guiding junior colleagues through complex analysis techniques while conveying why these approaches matter
  • Research teams developing shared understanding of ethical research practices through discussion and reflection
  • Professional associations creating communities of practice that transmit tacit knowledge and shared values
  • Client-researcher relationships where mutual understanding of research value develops over time
  • Peer review processes that provide feedback while reinforcing standards of research excellence

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine intersubjectivity in skilling through:

  • Replacing human mentors with automated guidance systems that cannot convey the intrinsic value of research skills
  • Creating disembodied research environments that limit opportunities for shared valuing of research capacities
  • Reducing opportunities for developing shared intentions between researchers through automated collaboration tools
  • Diminishing the role of social practices in skill development by providing instant answers rather than encouraging communal learning

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
The erosion of intersubjectivity in skilling has significant consequences for the market research industry:

  • Reduced transmission of tacit knowledge essential for research excellence
  • Weakening of shared understanding regarding research ethics and quality standards
  • Diminished development of social capacities necessary for collaborative research
  • Erosion of the research community's ability to collectively define and uphold professional values
  • Increased difficulty in onboarding new researchers as the entry-level-squeeze intensifies

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The challenge that different AI adoption measurement approaches yield dramatically different findings about AI's economic impact. As demonstrated by the contrast between exposure-based studies and spending-based research like the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, methodological choices fundamentally shape conclusions about AI's labor market effects.

docs.title: Evidence of Heterogeneity
docs.text:
Study Type Primary Method Key Employment Finding Example Exposure-based Occupational AI exposure scores Negative impact on entry-level jobs Brynjolfsson et al. (2025) Spending-based Observed AI vendor payments Positive impact at high intensity Ramp-Revelio study Survey-based Executive adoption surveys Mixed or positive impacts Yotzov et al. (2026)

The Ramp-Revelio study documents this heterogeneity through direct comparison: - Exposure-based studies predict job losses in high-exposure occupations - Spending-based research shows job growth among high-intensity adopters - The discrepancy stems from methodological differences, not contradictory realities

docs.title: Root Causes
docs.text: Three fundamental methodological differences drive these divergent findings:

docs.title: 1. Adoption Measurement
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Measure theoretical task feasibility ("could AI do this?")
  • Spending data: Measure actual adoption behavior ("is the firm paying for AI?")
  • Surveys: Capture self-reported usage ("do executives say they use AI?")

As the Ramp-Revelio study notes: "These estimates are closer to the Ramp–Revelio paid-adoption series than the firm-weighted BTOS benchmark, but they still measure a different object."

docs.title: 2. Intensity Dimension
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Typically binary or quintile-based
  • Spending data: Reveals continuous intensity effects (PEPM metric)
  • Surveys: Often lack precise intensity measures

The Ramp-Revelio study found only high-intensity adopters showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no change.

docs.title: 3. Selection Bias Handling
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Cannot distinguish adopters from non-adopters with identical workforce
  • Spending data: Enables direct comparison of adopters vs. later adopters
  • Surveys: Often lack pre-adoption data for comparison

The Ramp-Revelio study documents substantial pre-adoption differences that confound simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological heterogeneity creates critical challenges:

  • Conflicting guidance: Different studies recommend opposite actions based on methodology
  • Implementation uncertainty: Hard to predict AI impact without knowing intensity threshold
  • Evaluation complexity: Must select appropriate methodology for specific context
  • Vendor claims: AI providers may cite favorable methodology while ignoring others

docs.title: Strategic Response Framework
docs.text:
Market research organizations should adopt a methodologically sophisticated approach:

  1. Triangulate findings: Consider evidence from multiple methodological approaches
  2. Assess intensity: Focus on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact
  3. Control for selection: Account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI
  4. Contextualize results: Recognize sector-specific effects (e.g., concentrated in Information)

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This concept explains the contradictory findings between the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study (showing 12.0% entry-level growth) and exposure-based studies predicting job losses. It represents the methodological foundation for understanding the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and the value of the ai-adoption-methodological-innovation in spending-based measurement.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, navigating methodological heterogeneity requires: - Never relying on a single study's methodology for decision-making - Understanding the measurement approach behind any AI impact claim - Recognizing that "AI adoption" has no single empirical rate (as shown in Ramp-Revelio Figure 1) - Focusing on high-intensity implementation thresholds rather than binary adoption

Without this methodological sophistication, organizations risk making decisions based on incomplete or misleading evidence about AI's true impact.

docs.title: Narrow Field of Affordances
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-17 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A narrow field of affordances refers to an environment that provides limited action possibilities, restricting opportunities for the development and exercise of human capacities. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this concept is a key mechanism through which AI systems can create capacity-hostile environments.

docs.title: Core Characteristics
docs.text:
A narrow field of affordances exhibits these critical features:

  • Restricted action possibilities: Limits the range of activities users can engage in
  • Discouraged compensation: Makes it difficult for users to find alternative avenues to compensate for reduced capacity exercise
  • Systematic shrinkage: Represents a systematic, enduring, and deeply entrenched reduction in action possibilities
  • Cumulative effect: Results from the aggregation of multiple automated activities across different spheres

As Ferdman explains: "A narrow field of affordances is normatively problematic, from a structural point of view, when it leads to 'affordance shrinkage': when the reduction in action possibilities is systematic, enduring and deeply entrenched, such that discourages users from finding ways to compensate for the shrinkage."

docs.title: AI Automation and Affordance Shrinkage
docs.text:
AI systems contribute to narrow fields of affordances through:

  • Automation bias: Offloading tasks to AI reduces opportunities for habituation and skill development
  • Cumulative automation: Automating multiple everyday human activities across many spheres (writing, searching, planning, organizing, navigation, decision-making)
  • Discouraged exploration: Design features that discourage users from seeking new opportunities for growth and exploration
  • Reduced cognitive musculature: Depriving users of routine opportunities to practice judgment, leaving them unprepared for exceptional circumstances

As Ferdman states: "Automating routine tasks and leaving only exception-handling to the human user, 'deprives the user of the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature, leaving them atrophied and unprepared when the exceptions do arise' (Lee et al. 2025)."

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
In market research contexts, narrow fields of affordances manifest through:

  • AI tools that automate data collection and analysis, reducing opportunities for researchers to develop analytical judgment
  • Automated reporting systems that limit opportunities for creative presentation of findings
  • Recommendation engines that suggest research topics based on past behavior rather than encouraging novel question formulation
  • AI assistants that provide complete research protocols rather than supporting researcher self-deliberation

docs.title: Structural Implications
docs.text:
The concept of narrow fields of affordances has significant structural implications:

  • Capacity-hostile environments often feature narrow fields of affordances that systematically undermine capacity development
  • The cumulative effect of automation across multiple spheres creates environments where compensation for deskilling becomes increasingly difficult
  • Narrow fields of affordances contribute to the entry-level-squeeze by reducing foundational learning opportunities
  • Organizations must deliberately design capacity-conducive environments with rich affordance landscapes to counteract this trend

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) is a metric developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to measure the intensity of AI adoption at the firm level. It calculates monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after sustained AI adoption begins.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
PEPM = (Σ²ₘ₌₀ AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ) / (3 × HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁)

Where: - AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ = AI vendor spend for firm i in month m after adoption - HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁ = baseline headcount in the month before adoption

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. AI adoption is defined as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  2. PEPM is calculated using AI spend over the first three months after adoption begins
  3. Baseline headcount is measured in the month before adoption
  4. Firms are sorted into intensity groups:
  5. High intensity: top PEPM tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom two PEPM terciles

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
• Provides a direct, observed measure of AI adoption intensity rather than relying on occupational exposure scores
  • Allows researchers to distinguish between firms that adopt AI lightly versus intensively
  • Correlates closely with adoption of more complex AI products and tools (coding agents, APIs) versus simpler chat subscriptions
  • Enables analysis of differential impacts based on adoption intensity

docs.title: Key Findings Using PEPM
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters (top tercile) grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • Gains emerged gradually, suggesting a "learning curve" as firms integrated AI tools

docs.title: Plan-Forming vs Plan-Following
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-17 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Plan-forming vs plan-following refers to the critical distinction between actively creating plans through self-deliberation (requiring agential control) versus executing pre-determined plans (more habitual). As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this distinction has significant implications for AI's impact on capacity development.

docs.title: Plan-Forming
docs.text:
Plan-forming involves:

  • Self-deliberation: Actively considering values, goals, and circumstances to develop appropriate plans
  • Agential control: Full control over initiating the planning activity, including both settling function (deciding between options) and coordination function (organizing different types of plans)
  • Responsibility ownership: Taking accountability for plan outcomes, enabling self-critique and growth
  • Practical wisdom: Applying phronesis to determine effective means to ends and assess circumstances accurately

As Ferdman explains: "Forming a plan by self-deliberation requires exercising control over all the steps of the activity of forming the plan, including over initiating the two functions of planning: settling (deciding between options) and coordinating."

docs.title: Plan-Following
docs.text:
Plan-following involves:

  • Environmental triggers: Responding to recommendations or prompts from external sources
  • Habitual response: Executing plans without initiating the planning activity
  • Diminished responsibility: Ability to shift accountability for outcomes to the plan provider
  • Reduced practical wisdom development: Limited opportunities to develop judgment through trial and error

As Ferdman states: "Relying on an APA to form our plans for us is more like a habit that is developed in response to a trigger in the environment."

docs.title: AI Personal Assistants and the Shift
docs.text:
AI personal assistants (APAs) can shift users from plan-formers to plan-followers through:

  • Providing complete plans that users merely execute, rather than supporting self-deliberation
  • Constant availability that discourages users from seeking alternative growth opportunities
  • Offloading small-scale decisions that over time amount to broader life goals
  • Creating environments where users become acclimated to responding to APA outputs rather than exercising agential control

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
In market research contexts, this distinction manifests through:

  • Plan-forming: Researchers developing novel research approaches through self-deliberation on client needs, methodological considerations, and resource constraints
  • Plan-following: Researchers executing pre-constructed research protocols generated by AI tools without critical evaluation
  • Plan-forming: Analysts adjusting methodology in response to emerging data patterns through practical wisdom
  • Plan-following: Analysts rigidly following AI-recommended analysis paths without adaptation

docs.title: Implications for Capacity Development
docs.text:
The shift from plan-forming to plan-following has significant implications:

  • Reduced opportunities to develop practical rationality and phronesis
  • Diminished development of creative capacities needed for innovative research design
  • Weakened volitional capacity as researchers rely on external direction rather than self-motivation
  • Erosion of epistemic capacities as researchers outsource critical thinking to AI systems
  • Contribution to the human-operating-model-gap between AI capabilities and human capacity development

docs.title: Seniorised roles
docs.text: The phenomenon where entry-level roles increasingly demand skills traditionally required in senior positions due to AI adoption.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: Seniorised roles describe the accelerating trend where entry-level positions now require skills traditionally associated with senior roles, driven by AI automation of foundational tasks. Figure 8 in the PwC 2026 report provides compelling evidence: in the US top AI exposure quartile, seniorised entry-level job postings are projected to grow 35% between 2019-2025, while non-seniorised roles decline by 10%. This occurs because AI tools handle routine onboarding tasks (e.g., data entry for [[inventory-clerks]] or basic analysis for [[recruiters]]), compressing career ladders and elevating entry requirements. Common senior skills now appearing in entry-level descriptions include strategic decision-making frameworks, cross-departmental collaboration, client advisory capabilities, and complex problem-solving—particularly in high-growth professionalised-jobs. Figure 7 contextualizes this within broader market trends, showing high AI exposure quartile entry-level postings have flatlined since 2022, suggesting seniorisation may be a prerequisite for growth in AI-impacted roles. The report warns this trend could exacerbate early-career inequality if not balanced with structured mentorship, as new graduates face higher barriers without prior exposure to advanced skills. However, organizations using the ai-job-future-framework can mitigate risks by designing onboarding that combines AI tools with human skill development. The phenomenon represents a key manifestation of AI's impact on career progression, with implications for education systems needing to prepare students for accelerated responsibility in the AI era.

docs.title: Social Capacities
docs.text: First Observed: 2026-07-18 Last Updated: 2026-07-18

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Social capacities are the human capacities related to forming meaningful relationships, understanding others' perspectives, and participating in communal life, including moral capacity and relational capacity. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are essential for ethical research practices and constitute a core component of human flourishing in market research contexts.

docs.title: Moral Capacity
docs.text:
• Ability to make ethical judgments and act accordingly in research contexts
  • Includes recognizing ethical dilemmas and applying moral reasoning
  • Essential for maintaining research integrity and participant welfare
  • Critical for navigating complex ethical challenges in sensitive research topics

docs.title: Relational Capacity
docs.text:
• Ability to form meaningful relationships of friendship, trust, and professional collaboration
  • Includes understanding others' perspectives and building rapport
  • Essential for effective client relationships and team collaboration
  • Critical for qualitative research methods requiring deep participant engagement

As Ferdman explains: "The social capacities include the moral capacity as well as the social and caring capacities for developing meaningful relationships of friendship and love."

docs.title: Role in Life-Planning and Research
docs.text:
Social capacities play a critical role in both life-planning and market research:

  • Planning involves coordinating with others toward achieving complex research goals
  • Social relationships provide reasons for action that inform research goals (e.g., being a good researcher, contributing to knowledge)
  • Ethical research practices depend on moral capacity to protect participant welfare
  • Building rapport with research participants requires relational capacity
  • Team collaboration depends on shared understanding and mutual respect

docs.title: Threats from AI Systems
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine social capacities through:

  • Reducing opportunities for embodied interaction critical for developing moral attention
  • Diminishing mentor-mentee relationships essential for transmitting research ethics
  • Creating disembodied research environments that limit opportunities for relationship building
  • Replacing human-to-human interaction in customer interviews and focus groups
  • Reducing opportunities to develop shared valuing of research ethics through social practices

As Ferdman notes: "Without being embodied in a social interaction—without the return of the gaze of the other—we would be hard-pressed to recognize them spontaneously as moral agents."

docs.title: Examples in Market Research
docs.text:
In market research contexts, social capacities manifest through:

  • Moral capacity in ensuring informed consent and protecting participant privacy
  • Relational capacity in building rapport with research participants during interviews
  • Ethical judgment in navigating conflicts of interest with clients
  • Team collaboration that depends on shared understanding of research values
  • Client relationships built on trust and mutual respect

docs.title: Implications for the Industry
docs.text:
The erosion of social capacities has significant implications for market research:

  • Reduced ability to conduct ethical research that protects participant welfare
  • Diminished quality of qualitative research that depends on human rapport
  • Weakened client relationships due to reduced relational capacity
  • Erosion of research community standards when shared valuing of ethics diminishes
  • Contribution to the human-operating-model-gap between AI capabilities and human social skills
